items.caption: A parabola passes, a circle fails
items.text: Each dashed line holds x fixed. On the parabola y = x² − 1 every such line meets the curve exactly once, so each input has one output. On the circle x² + y² = 4 the line x = 1 meets it at y = √3 and y = −√3: one input, two outputs, so the circle is not the graph of a function.

items.caption: Reading the period from two peaks
items.text: The graph of sin x from 0 to 4π. The stretch from 0 to 2π is one complete cycle, and the stretch from 2π to 4π repeats it exactly. Measuring between two consecutive peaks, at π/2 and 5π/2, gives the same 2π — any pair of matching points one cycle apart does.

items.caption: f(x) = e^(−x): the curve flattens onto y = 0
items.text: Toward the right the curve sinks ever closer to the dashed line y = 0 without touching it: that line is a horizontal asymptote, and it is the end behaviour of the function written as a level. Toward the left the curve climbs without bound instead. Scan the far ends of any family on the

items.caption: Adding outputs, one input at a time
items.text: f(x) = x² and g(x) = 5x − 3 from the text, with their sum. At x = 2 the bar for f(2) = 4 rises from the axis and the bar for g(2) = 7 sits on top of it; together they reach 11, exactly where the f + g curve passes. Every point of f + g is built the same way: same input, outputs added.

items.caption: Where a product vanishes
items.text: f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = x − 3 multiply to (fg)(x) = x² − x − 6. Two lines make a parabola, and its zeros are inherited: fg = 0 at x = −2, where f is zero, and at x = 3, where g is zero. Between them one factor is positive and the other negative, so the product dips below the axis.

items.caption: A hole where the divisor is zero
items.text: (x² − 1)/(x + 1) simplifies to x − 1, and the graph is that line — with one point missing. At x = −1 the divisor g(x) = x + 1 is zero, so the quotient has no value there, even though the simplified formula would give −2. The open circle marks the input the simplification hides.

items.caption: The overlap of two domains
items.text: √x needs x ≥ 0 and √(4 − x) needs x ≤ 4. A sum, difference or product needs both functions defined at the same input, so its domain is where the two lines overlap: [0, 4]. Outside it, at least one part has no value.

items.caption: f composed with itself
items.text: Applying the same rule twice gives a new curve, f(f(x)), drawn beside f: the second application acts on the outputs of the first. Repeating a function is how iteration and recursion begin. See how the shape changes with each extra application on the

items.caption: f(x) = eˆx, g(x) = ln x: f(g(x)) = x
items.text: Composed in either order the two curves collapse onto the line y = x: the logarithm undoes the exponential and the exponential undoes the logarithm, which is the defining property of an inverse pair drawn out. The only trace of the pair is the domain restriction x > 0 inherited from ln. Check any candidate pair the same way on the

items.caption: Two graph readings, one composition
items.text: To find (f ∘ g)(0) from graphs: on the graph of g, go from x = 0 to the curve and read g(0) = −2. That output is the next input — find −2 on the x-axis of f's graph, go up to the curve and read f(−2) = 5. Every point of f ∘ g takes this pair of readings.

items.caption: Nothing to rule out
items.text: A line like f(x) = 2x has no division, no root and no logarithm, so no input can fail: the graph runs on forever in both directions and every real number on the x-axis has a point above or below it. The domain is (−∞, ∞). Compare functions with real restrictions on the

items.page: Domain of a Function - How to Find It
items.caption: What the formula allows, what the situation allows
items.text: The projectile's height formula h(t) = −16t² + 64t gives an output for every real t, so its natural domain is all real numbers. The situation keeps only the flight itself: from launch at t = 0 to landing at t = 4. The restricted domain [0, 4] is a choice made outside the formula, sitting inside the natural domain.

items.caption: A straight line, constant slope
items.text: f(x) = x, the simplest member of the linear family. Every step of 1 to the right rises by the same amount, so the graph is a straight line; changing m tilts it and changing b slides it up or down, but it never bends. See the other families side by side on the

items.caption: f(x) = 0.3x² − 3: a parabola
items.text: The U-shape opens upward because the leading coefficient is positive, the vertex sits at the minimum on the axis of symmetry x = 0, and the two x-intercepts are where the curve crosses the axis. Every quadratic has this shape, stretched, flipped or shifted. Change the coefficients and watch the vertex and intercepts move on the

items.caption: A cubic with a peak and a valley
items.text: f(x) = 0.2x³ − 2x. The ends go in opposite directions, as for every cubic with a positive leading coefficient, and between them the curve turns twice: a local maximum, then a local minimum. A cubic has at most two such turns. Compare it with the other families on the

items.caption: f(x) = 1/x: two branches and two asymptotes
items.text: The graph breaks at x = 0, where the denominator is zero, into two branches that hug the axes without touching them: the vertical asymptote x = 0 and the horizontal asymptote y = 0. Both are marked. Rational functions are the family where asymptotes are the rule rather than the exception. Compare it with the other families on the

items.caption: Starts at the origin, grows ever more slowly
items.text: f(x) = √x is defined only for x ≥ 0, so the graph begins at the origin and runs to the right. It keeps rising, but each step adds less than the one before: the curve flattens without ever levelling off. Compare it with the other families on the

items.caption: f(x) = |x|: a V with its corner at the origin
items.text: Two straight rays of slopes −1 and 1 meet at a corner: the graph is the distance from zero, never negative, and symmetric about the y-axis. The corner is the one point with no tangent line. Set it beside the parabola, which it resembles from afar, on the

items.caption: Constant pieces with a jump
items.text: The Heaviside step: 0 for negative inputs, 1 from 0 on. Each piece is a horizontal segment and the graph jumps between them — the pattern every step function shares, from this single jump to the floor function's staircase of jumps at every integer. Build other piecewise functions on the

items.caption: f(x) = 2ˆx: doubling with each unit step
items.text: The curve hugs the x-axis on the left, passes through (0, 1), and climbs faster and faster to the right: each unit step in x doubles the height. It never reaches zero and has no maximum. Change the base to see growth turn into decay on the

items.caption: The logarithm's vertical wall
items.text: f(x) = ln(x) exists only for x > 0. Near 0 it plunges without bound along the y-axis, it crosses the x-axis at x = 1, and to the right it keeps climbing, more and more slowly. It is the exponential graph reflected across y = x. Compare it with the other families on the

items.caption: f(x) = sin x: a wave of period 2π
items.text: The curve oscillates between −1 and 1 and repeats every 2π, crossing the axis at every multiple of π. It is the model of periodic behaviour, and the cosine beside it is the same wave shifted a quarter period. Compare the trigonometric family with the others on the

items.caption: Four quadrants, one plotted point
items.text: The section's own example, (3, −2). Start at the origin, move 3 units right along the x-axis, then 2 units down. A positive x and a negative y put the point in Quadrant IV: each quadrant is named by the signs of its two coordinates.

items.caption: One function can be run backwards, the other cannot
items.text: Doubling sends −1, 0 and 3 to −2, 0 and 6, and every output has exactly one arrow coming in, so each arrow can be followed back: f⁻¹(6) = 3. Squaring sends both 3 and −3 to 9; standing at 9 there are two arrows to retrace and no rule for choosing, so x² on all real numbers has no inverse.

items.secTitle: Inverse as Reflection over y = x
items.caption: Coordinates swapped, points mirrored
items.text: The section's two points: (2, 5) on f becomes (5, 2) on f⁻¹, and (−1, 3) becomes (3, −1). Each pair is joined by a segment that meets the dashed line y = x at a right angle, halfway between the two points: that is exactly a reflection across y = x. A point already on the line, such as (4, 4), is its own swap and does not move.

items.caption: The parabola fails, the cubic passes
items.text: On the parabola, the line y = 4 crosses at x = −2 and x = 2: two inputs share the output 4, so the inverse would not know which to return. Every horizontal line meets the cubic exactly once, so each output comes from one input and f⁻¹(x) = ∛x is well defined.

items.caption: f(x) = x² restricted to x ≥ 0: inverse √x
items.text: The full parabola fails the horizontal line test, so only its right half is kept, drawn solid; that half is one-to-one and its reflection in y = x is the square root. The left half, faint, is the part given up to make the inverse exist. See the restriction and the resulting inverse on the

items.caption: f(x) = eˆx and f⁻¹(x) = ln x
items.text: The exponential and the logarithm are mirror images in y = x: the exponential’s horizontal asymptote y = 0 becomes the logarithm’s vertical asymptote x = 0, and the point (0, 1) becomes (1, 0). Domain and range have traded places. Compare the other classic pairs on the

items.caption: One function, two formulas
items.text: The section's example: x + 1 for x < 0 (blue) and x² for x ≥ 0 (navy). Each input falls in exactly one interval, so exactly one formula runs: f(−3) = −2 from the first, f(2) = 4 from the second. At the boundary x = 0 the condition x ≥ 0 applies, so f(0) = 0; the first piece’s end at (0, 1) is open and never used.

items.caption: Collecting the outputs of each piece
items.text: The constant piece outputs only 2; the line x + 1, starting at (0, 1) with a solid dot, outputs every value from 1 upward. The amber bar on the y-axis is the union of the two: 2 already lies in [1, ∞), so the range is [1, ∞).

items.caption: x + 1 for x < 0, x − 1 for x ≥ 0: a jump at 0
items.text: The two pieces meet the boundary x = 0 at different heights, 1 from the left and −1 from the right, so the graph jumps; the open dot marks the value the left piece approaches but does not take, the closed dot the value the function actually has. Continuity at the boundary would need the two dots to coincide. Move the pieces until they meet on the

items.caption: |x| as two pieces: −x then x
items.text: The left ray is the line y = −x on x < 0 and the right ray is y = x on x ≥ 0; the two pieces meet at the origin at the same height, so the V is continuous even though its formula changes there. The closed dot at 0 belongs to the right piece. Rebuild the V from its two pieces on the

items.caption: The Heaviside step: −1 then 1
items.text: Each piece is a constant, so the graph is two horizontal segments with a jump of 2 at x = 0; the open and closed dots record which piece owns the boundary. Every step function is built this way, one flat piece per interval. Try the three-piece sign function on the

items.caption: The plumber's charge as a graph
items.text: C(t) = 50 for 0 < t ≤ 1 and 30t + 20 for t > 1. The flat piece is the first-hour charge; after the threshold at one hour, the line climbs $30 per hour. Both pieces give $50 at t = 1, so the graph has no jump, and three hours cost C(3) = $110.

items.caption: f(x) = x³: symmetric about the origin
items.text: Rotating the picture half a turn about the origin returns it to itself: the point (x, y) has the partner (−x, −y) on the curve, which is f(−x) = −f(x). That is an odd function; the parabola beside it in the tool is the even case instead. Test any family for both symmetries on the

items.caption: f(x) = x²: symmetric about the y-axis
items.text: The reflection of the parabola across the y-axis lands exactly on the parabola: f(−x) = f(x). A graph symmetric about the origin, like x³, or symmetric about neither, like x² + x, can be checked the same way. Fold any curve along the axis or spin it about the origin on the

items.caption: f(x) = x³: every horizontal line meets it once
items.text: The cubic passes the horizontal line test, so it is one-to-one and its inverse, the cube root, exists and is drawn as the mirror image in y = x. A parabola would fail the test, two inputs sharing one output, and would need its domain cut before an inverse could be drawn. Compare the two on the

items.caption: f(x) = eˆx: the outputs never reach 0 or below
items.text: The band on the y-axis marks the heights the curve reaches: everything above 0, with an open dot at 0 itself, and nothing at or below it. As a map from ℝ to ℝ, eˆx is therefore not onto: the negative half of the codomain is never hit. Shrink the codomain to (0, ∞) and the same function is onto. Compare the ranges of other families on the

items.caption: Falling, then rising
items.text: The section's example f(x) = x². Read from left to right, the curve falls until the vertex at x = 0 and rises after it. The direction is stated as x-intervals under the plot: decreasing on (−∞, 0], increasing on [0, ∞).

items.caption: eˆx and ln x: both only ever rise
items.text: Neither curve turns back anywhere: eˆx rises across all real inputs and ln x across all positive ones, so both are strictly increasing, hence monotonic. That is exactly why each can be undone, and the two are mirror images in the dashed line y = x: each is the other’s inverse. Explore other inverse pairs on the

items.caption: f(x) = sin x: every output between −1 and 1
items.text: However far the wave runs in either direction, its heights stay inside the band from −1 to 1 on the y-axis, both ends reached and marked with closed dots. So sin x is bounded above by 1 and below by −1; the band is its whole range. See which families are bounded on the

items.caption: A cubic’s peak and valley
items.text: The curve 0.2x³ − 2x rises to a peak, falls through the origin into a valley, then rises for good. The peak is a local maximum and the valley a local minimum: each is extreme only among nearby points, since the curve climbs higher than the peak further right and falls lower than the valley further left. Compare the shapes of other families on the

items.caption: f(x) = 1/x: vertical x = 0 and horizontal y = 0
items.text: The two dashed lines are the asymptotes: the curve runs off to infinity beside the vertical one and flattens onto the horizontal one at both ends, approaching each without touching. The vertical line marks a forbidden input, the horizontal one a limiting output. Explore oblique asymptotes as well on the

items.caption: The leading term decides the ends
items.text: The section's polynomial 3x⁴ − 5x² + 2 (solid) next to its leading term 3x⁴ (dashed). Near the origin the two differ, but as |x| grows the lower-degree terms stop mattering and the curves run together: even degree with a positive leading coefficient, so both ends rise without bound.

items.caption: f(x) = sin x repeats every 2π
items.text: Any stretch of the curve of length 2π is a copy of every other such stretch: that is periodicity, and 2π is the smallest length that works. The values never leave [−1, 1], so the function is also bounded. Compare with the non-periodic families on the

items.caption: Crossing and touching zeros
items.text: f(x) = (x + 1)(x − 2)² has two zeros. The factor x + 1 appears once, so at x = −1 the graph passes through the axis and changes sign. The factor x − 2 appears twice, so at x = 2 the graph touches the axis and turns back without changing sign.

items.caption: Average rate of change as a slope
items.text: The section's example: f(x) = x² on [1, 3]. The output climbs from 1 to 9, a rise of 8, while the input moves from 1 to 3, a run of 2. The ratio 8 / 2 = 4 is the slope of the secant line joining (1, 1) and (3, 9), the amber line.

items.caption: Bending down, then bending up
items.text: The section's cubic f(x) = x³. Left of the origin the curve lies below its tangent line (dashed, drawn at x = −1): concave down. Right of the origin it lies above its tangent (dashed, at x = 1): concave up. The switch happens at the origin, the inflection point.

items.caption: The domain shapes the range
items.text: The section's third example: the rule x² kept only on the domain [1, 3] (solid), with the rest of the parabola faint. The outputs start at f(1) = 1 and end at f(3) = 9, both reached, so the range is the closed interval [1, 9] marked on the y-axis, far smaller than the [0, ∞) of the full parabola.

items.caption: f(x) = x³: the range is the whole codomain
items.text: The band on the y-axis covers every height: each real number is the cube of some real number, so the range of x³ equals its codomain ℝ and the function is onto. For x², by contrast, the band stops at 0 and the negative half of the codomain is never reached. Compare the two on the

items.caption: f(x) = 1/x: every output except 0
items.text: Solving y = 1/x for x gives x = 1/y, which works for every y except 0, and the graph agrees: the band covers the whole y-axis with a single open dot at 0. The section's 1/(x − 3) is this curve moved 3 to the right, which leaves the heights, and so the range (−∞, 0) ∪ (0, ∞), unchanged. See it on the

items.caption: f(x) = eˆx: approaching 0, never reaching it
items.text: eˆx only increases, and as x runs left its outputs sink toward the horizontal asymptote y = 0 without ever arriving. So 0 is the edge of the range but not part of it: the band is (0, ∞), with an open dot at 0. The asymptote marks the boundary; the open dot records that it is never achieved. Compare bounded and unbounded families on the

items.caption: f(x) = x²: range [0, ∞) read off the y-axis
items.text: The shaded band on the vertical axis marks the heights the curve actually reaches: from the vertex at 0, included as a closed dot, upward without bound, and nothing below. Range is the vertical shadow of the graph. Switch to sin x and watch the band shrink to [−1, 1] on the

items.caption: f(x) = |x|: outputs from 0 upward
items.text: The V never dips below the axis, so its vertical band starts at 0 with a closed dot and runs upward: the same range as the parabola although the shape is different. Families with a minimum share this pattern; families with a horizontal asymptote, like eˆx, have an open endpoint instead. Compare them on the

items.caption: g(x) = f(x) + 3: the parabola and its range move up by 3
items.text: Adding 3 to every output lifts the whole graph by 3, so the range [0, ∞) of x² becomes [3, ∞): vertical transformations act directly on the range. A horizontal shift would leave the range alone. Move the parameter k and watch the lowest point rise and fall on the

items.caption: eˆx and ln x: range and domain trade places
items.text: The outputs of eˆx fill (0, ∞); reflected in the dashed line y = x, those same values become the inputs of ln x, whose domain is (0, ∞). In the other direction, every real input of eˆx reappears as an output of ln x, so its range is all of ℝ. Watch the swap for other pairs on the

items.caption: All four parameters at once
items.text: The dashed curve is the parent f(x) = x²; the solid one is g(x) = 0.5 · f(1.5(x − 2)) + 1. Inside the function, h = 2 moves the vertex right and b = 1.5 narrows the curve; outside, a = 0.5 flattens it and k = 1 lifts it. The vertex lands at (2, 1). Set each of a, b, h, k yourself on the

items.caption: g(x) = f(x) + 3
items.text: The dashed parabola is f(x) = x² and the solid one is the same curve lifted 3 units: every point moved straight up by the same amount, the vertex included, and the shape is untouched. A negative k would push it down. Drag k through negative values on the

items.caption: g(x) = f(x − 3)
items.text: Subtracting 3 inside the function moves the parabola 3 units to the right, the direction opposite to the sign: the vertex that was at 0 now sits at 3. The graph itself is unchanged, only its position. Watch the vertex slide as h changes on the

items.caption: g(x) = −x²: reflected in the x-axis
items.text: Negating the output flips the parabola upside down across the x-axis: points above the axis land the same distance below it, and the vertex stays on the axis. The mirror line is drawn in the picture. Reflect other families in the same line on the

items.caption: g(x) = √(−x): reflected in the y-axis
items.text: Negating the input mirrors the square root across the y-axis: the curve that rose to the right now rises to the left, and its domain [0, ∞) becomes (−∞, 0]. An even function would be its own reflection here. Reflect the other families in the y-axis on the

items.caption: g(x) = 2f(x)
items.text: Multiplying every output by 2 doubles each height: the parabola becomes narrower because it climbs twice as fast, while its x-intercept and vertex on the axis stay put. A factor between 0 and 1 would flatten it instead. Slide a past 1 and below 1 on the

items.caption: g(x) = f(2x)
items.text: Doubling the input compresses the graph horizontally by a factor of 2: the height that x² reaches at x = 2 is now reached at x = 1. Heights are unchanged; positions along the x-axis are halved. Compare with the vertical stretch, which looks similar but moves different points, on the

items.caption: Four transformations, one parabola
items.text: The section's example g(x) = −2(x + 3)² + 5 against its parent x² (dashed). Shifting left 3 and up 5 carries the vertex from (0, 0) to (−3, 5); the factor −2 makes the curve twice as steep and turns it upside down, so the vertex becomes a maximum.

items.text: The section's parabola: its vertex at (3, −2) gives h = 3 and k = −2. One step right of the vertex the graph has dropped 2 units, where the parent x² would have risen 1, so |a| = 2 and, since it opens downward, a = −2. The point (4, −4) checks the result: −2(4 − 3)² − 2 = −4.

items.caption: ln(x), frozen
items.text: One red wall at x = 0, approached from the right only — and no flattening anywhere: the climb never ends.

items.caption: tan(x), frozen
items.text: Red walls at every π/2 + nπ, each branch sweeping the full height between its two fences.

items.caption: e⁻ˣ, frozen
items.text: The curve hugs the green line y = 0 ever more tightly to the right — and ignores it completely to the left.

items.caption: 1/(1 + x²), frozen
items.text: One symmetric hump, both tails sliding down to the same green floor — and no wall anywhere.

items.caption: arctan(x), frozen
items.text: Two different green ceilings: −π/2 catching the left tail, +π/2 catching the right.

items.caption: 1/(1 + e⁻ˣ), frozen
items.text: The S-curve boxed between its floor y = 0 and ceiling y = 1, crossing the midline at (0, ½).

items.caption: 1/x, frozen
items.text: The archetype: red wall at x = 0, green floor at y = 0, two branches pinned between them.

items.caption: (x + 1)/(x − 1), frozen
items.text: The same hyperbola structure moved off the axes: wall at x = 1, level at y = 1.

items.caption: x/(x² − 1), frozen
items.text: Two red walls at x = ±1 cut the curve into three branches; the middle one crosses the green floor at the origin.

items.caption: x + 1/x, frozen
items.text: The purple slant y = x catches both far ends while the red wall at x = 0 separates the branches.

items.caption: (x² − 1)/x, frozen
items.text: Divided out, this is x − 1/x: the same purple slant, approached from the mirror side.

items.caption: f(x) = x, domain frozen
items.text: The identity line over one unbroken green band: every real input accepted, none changed.

items.caption: f(x) = 2x, domain frozen
items.text: The doubled line f(x) = 2x over a full green band — scaling an input is never a reason to refuse it.

items.caption: f(x) = x², domain frozen
items.text: The parabola over a solid green band: inputs unrestricted, even though outputs never go negative.

items.caption: f(x) = x³, domain frozen
items.text: The cubic over a full green band — unrestricted in domain and range alike.

items.caption: f(x) = eˣ, domain frozen
items.text: eˣ over a full green band: any exponent is welcome, however negative, and the answer is just very small.

items.caption: f(x) = sin(x), domain frozen
items.text: The endless wave over an endless green band — any angle, wound any number of times.

items.caption: f(x) = cos(x), domain frozen
items.text: The same full-domain picture as sine, shifted a quarter period.

items.caption: f(x) = |x|, domain frozen
items.text: The V over a solid green band: the corner at zero is a smoothness issue, not a domain one.

items.secTitle: The Logarithm and Its Open Boundary
items.caption: ln(x), domain frozen
items.text: Red band to the left, green strictly to the right, and the open circle at x = 0 recording the refusal: the boundary point itself is not allowed.

items.secTitle: The Square Root and Its Closed Boundary
items.caption: √x, domain frozen
items.text: The filled green dot at the origin is the difference: zero is accepted, the curve genuinely starts there. Domain [0, ∞).

items.secTitle: The Reciprocal and Its Excluded Point
items.caption: 1/x, domain frozen
items.text: Green in both directions with one puncture: a lone open circle at x = 0, the single refused input that shapes the whole graph.

items.caption: f(x) = x, range frozen
items.text: One unbroken green band up the y-axis: every height is an output, each hit exactly once.

items.caption: f(x) = 2x, range frozen
items.text: Full green band: doubling covers every output, just twice as fast.

items.caption: f(x) = x³, range frozen
items.text: Odd power, full coverage: from arbitrarily deep to arbitrarily high, nothing on the y-axis is missed.

items.caption: f(x) = ln(x), range frozen
items.text: The curve lives only on the right half-plane, yet the green band covers the entire y-axis — restricted domain, complete range.

items.caption: f(x) = x², range frozen
items.text: Green from zero upward with a filled dot at the floor: 0 is genuinely attained at the vertex; below it, red.

items.caption: f(x) = |x|, range frozen
items.text: The same range as the parabola — [0, ∞), floor attained at the corner — from a different shape.

items.caption: f(x) = √x, range frozen
items.text: Range [0, ∞), floor attained at the origin — and each output reached exactly once.

items.caption: f(x) = eˣ, range frozen
items.text: Green above zero with an OPEN circle at the floor: the curve presses toward y = 0 forever without producing it.

items.caption: f(x) = sin(x), range frozen
items.text: A green band from −1 to 1 with filled dots at both walls — the extremes are real outputs, hit once per period.

items.caption: f(x) = cos(x), range frozen
items.text: The identical band to sine : range cannot tell the two apart — the phase difference lives on the x-axis.

items.secTitle: The Reciprocal and Its Missing Output
items.caption: f(x) = 1/x, range frozen
items.text: Green in both directions with one puncture at y = 0: the single output no input can produce.

items.caption: x²: even, frozen
items.text: Amber f(−x) hides under the blue curve — the mirror image IS the function — while teal −f(x) hangs separate.

items.caption: |x|: even, frozen
items.text: Both arms mirror across the y-axis; amber under blue, the teal flip pointing down. The corner sits on the axis of symmetry itself.

items.caption: cos(x): even, frozen
items.text: Amber vanished under blue along the whole wave; the teal flip rides half a period out of phase.

items.caption: x: odd, frozen
items.text: Amber and teal fuse into one line — f(−x) and −f(x) are literally the same — mirroring the blue identity.

items.caption: x³: odd, frozen
items.text: Amber f(−x) and teal −f(x) trace one shared curve: the blue original’s half-turn twin.

items.caption: sin(x): odd, frozen
items.text: Every right-side crest matched by a left-side trough; amber and teal share one curve.

items.caption: 1/x: odd, frozen
items.text: The two branches rotate onto each other about the origin — symmetry surviving a hole at its own center.

items.caption: √x: neither, frozen
items.text: Blue on the right, amber marooned on the left, teal below: three curves with no common ground — the domain never allowed the test.

items.caption: eˣ: neither, frozen
items.text: Growth, decay, and negative growth — three genuinely different curves, no overlap anywhere.

items.caption: ln(x): neither, frozen
items.text: Blue right, amber left, teal diving — no two curves even share a domain.

items.caption: x² + x: neither, frozen
items.text: Three distinct parabolas: the even term keeps its sign, the odd term flips, and the mixture agrees with nothing.

items.caption: y = x, tangent at x₀ = 2
items.text: The dashed amber tangent lies exactly on the blue line: a line is its own best linear approximation, everywhere.

items.caption: y = 2x, tangent at x₀ = 1
items.text: Constant slope 2: one tangent serves every point, coinciding with the curve itself.

items.caption: x², tangent at x₀ = 1.5
items.text: Slope 2x₀ = 3 at the frozen point; drag left and the tangent tilts down through the horizontal rest at the vertex.

items.caption: x³, tangent at x₀ = 1
items.text: Slope 3x₀² = 3 — and never negative anywhere: every cubic tangent points weakly uphill.

items.caption: 1/x, tangent at x₀ = 1
items.text: Slope −1 at (1, 1); the tangent and the axes enclose a triangle of area 2 — the same area from every tangent point.

items.caption: eˣ, tangent at x₀ = 1
items.text: Height e, slope e: the tangent’s steepness equals the curve’s value at every point.

items.caption: ln(x), tangent at x₀ = 2
items.text: Slope 1/x₀ = ½: gentle out here, rearing toward vertical as the point approaches the wall at zero.

items.caption: √x, tangent at x₀ = 4
items.text: Slope ¼ at (4, 2) — and an endpoint drama off-screen left: the tangent turns vertical at x = 0.

items.caption: |x|, tangent at x₀ = 2
items.text: The dashed tangent coincides with the right arm; at the corner itself, no single line fits and the tangent fails.

items.caption: sin(x), tangent at x₀ = 0
items.text: Slope cos(0) = 1: the tangent is y = x — the small-angle approximation drawn as geometry.

items.caption: cos(x), tangent at x₀ = π/2
items.text: Caught at its steepest descent: slope −sin(π/2) = −1 as the wave crosses zero.

items.caption: x-axis flip, frozen
items.text: The parabola and its upside-down twin pinching together at the origin — roots are the fixed points of this mirror.

items.caption: y-axis flip, frozen
items.text: √x lives on the right; √(−x) lives entirely on the left — the mirror relocated the domain itself.

items.secTitle: Reflection Across the Line y = x
items.caption: Diagonal mirror, frozen
items.text: Reflecting x² across the amber diagonal stacks two branches over each input — a multivalued inverse, both branches drawn.

items.caption: Mirror at y = 1, frozen
items.text: The parabola and its reflection 2 − x² crossing exactly on the amber line — the fixed points where f(x) = c.

items.caption: Mirror at x = 1, frozen
items.text: Two square roots opening toward each other, meeting on the vertical amber mirror.

items.caption: |f(x)|, frozen
items.text: The rectified sine: every dip bounced upward, corners where the wave used to cross zero.

items.caption: f(|x|), frozen
items.text: A left half conjured from nothing: √|x| mirrors the right branch of √x into a fully even curve.

items.caption: a = 2, frozen
items.text: Every height doubled: same vertex, same roots, twice the climb. The gray original shows what the blue curve left behind.

items.caption: k = 3, frozen
items.text: The whole parabola lifted rigidly by 3 — shape untouched, vertex now at (0, 3), roots gone above the axis.

items.caption: b = 2, frozen
items.text: Input doubled means the curve narrows: each height reached at half the distance — the famous backwards behavior.

items.caption: h = 3, frozen
items.text: Subtracting 3 inside the parentheses slides the curve right: the vertex now lives at x = 3.

items.caption: All four at once, frozen
items.text: Widened by a = 0.5, narrowed by b = 1.5, carried to (2, 1) by the shifts — the full template in one picture.

items.caption: f(x) = x, frozen
items.text: The identity line at default parameters: slope 1, intercept 0 — through the origin, climbing one unit up for every unit right.

items.caption: f(x) = 0.3x² − 3, frozen
items.text: A wide upward bowl with its vertex at (0, −3); the two axis crossings near ±3.16 are the roots the discriminant promises.

items.caption: f(x) = 0.2x³ − 2x, frozen
items.text: Ends running opposite ways, two turning points, and an inflection at the origin — the full odd-degree signature in one window.

items.caption: f(x) = x², frozen
items.text: At n = 2 the family wears its parabola disguise; dragging the exponent replays polynomials, reciprocals, and roots in this same window.

items.caption: f(x) = 1/x, frozen
items.text: Two branches split by the vertical asymptote at x = 0, each flattening toward y = 0 as it runs away from the pole.

items.caption: f(x) = 2ˣ, frozen
items.text: Doubling with every step right, hugging the axis to the left — runaway growth on one side, an asymptote on the other.

items.caption: f(x) = ln(x), frozen
items.text: Nothing exists left of the asymptote at x = 0; the curve crosses at x = 1, then climbs forever at an ever-slowing pace.

items.caption: f(x) = sin(x), frozen
items.text: Three full cycles of the pure wave: period 2π, bounded between −1 and 1, zeros at every multiple of π.

items.caption: f(x) = cos(x), frozen
items.text: The same wave as sine arriving a quarter period early: maximum at x = 0 and mirror symmetry across the y-axis.

items.caption: f(x) = tan(x), frozen
items.text: Strictly increasing branches sweeping from −∞ to +∞ between red asymptotes spaced π apart.

items.caption: f(x) = |x|, frozen
items.text: Two straight arms meeting in a sharp corner at the origin — continuous everywhere, differentiable everywhere but there.

items.caption: f(x) = √x, frozen
items.text: A curve that starts vertically at the origin and flattens forever — with nothing at all to its left.

items.caption: Identity ∘ quadratic, frozen
items.text: Both compositions collapse onto the same parabola — the identity passes x² through untouched from either seat.

items.caption: x² and sin(x), both orders
items.text: Blue: (sin x)² folded positive at doubled frequency. Amber: sin(x²) accelerating outward. Same ingredients, different seats.

items.caption: x³ and sin(x), both orders
items.text: Blue: (sin x)³ keeps its sign pattern, squashed toward the axis. Amber: sin(x³) oscillates ever faster. Both curves odd.

items.caption: 1/x and sin(x), both orders
items.text: Blue: 1/sin(x) — asymptotes at every multiple of π. Amber: sin(1/x) — infinitely fast oscillation packed against x = 0.

items.caption: eˣ and sin(x), both orders
items.text: Blue: e^(sin x) breathing between 1/e and e, always positive. Amber: sin(eˣ) flat on the left, frantic on the right.

items.caption: ln(x) and x², both orders
items.text: Blue: ln(x²) — two mirrored branches, the domain doubled by the inner square. Amber: (ln x)² — a valley bottoming at x = 1, half-line only.

items.caption: sin(x) and x², both orders
items.text: Blue: sin(x²) — bounded but accelerating. Amber: (sin x)² — steady rhythm, values folded positive.

items.caption: cos(x) and x², both orders
items.text: Blue: cos(x²) ripples out symmetrically from its peak at the origin. Amber: (cos x)² traces the power-reduction identity.

items.caption: |x| and sin(x), both orders
items.text: Blue: |sin x| creased along the x-axis — the rectified wave. Amber: sin|x| creased along the y-axis — the mirrored wave.

items.caption: √x and sin(x), both orders
items.text: Blue: √(sin x) survives only on the positive arches. Amber: sin(√x) lives on x ≥ 0 and slows as it goes.

items.secTitle: The Inverse Pair: Exponential and Logarithm
items.caption: eˣ ∘ ln(x) and ln ∘ eˣ, frozen
items.text: Both compositions collapse onto y = x — blue on the positive half-line only, amber across the whole axis. Inverses, with their domains showing.

items.secTitle: The Square and the Square Root
items.caption: √(x²) versus (√x)², frozen
items.text: Blue: √(x²) = |x| — the V, everywhere. Amber: (√x)² = x — the identity, but only for x ≥ 0. Half an inverse pair.

items.caption: x² ∘ x², frozen
items.text: Squaring twice gives x⁴: flatter valley, steeper walls — and the blue and amber curves coincide exactly, since order cannot matter.

items.caption: f(x) = x, frozen
items.text: Curve, inverse, and mirror in one line: the identity is the fixed point of reflection itself.

items.secTitle: The Scaled Linear Function and Its Inverse
items.caption: 2x and x/2, frozen
items.text: Two lines with reciprocal slopes, reflecting into each other across the dashed mirror.

items.secTitle: The Cubic and the Cube Root
items.caption: x³ and ∛x, frozen
items.text: A full inverse pair with no restriction anywhere: the cubic never turns around, so the cube root accepts every real input.

items.caption: 1/x, self-inverse, frozen
items.text: The dashed amber curve retraces the blue hyperbola exactly: flipping a fraction twice restores it.

items.caption: eˣ and ln(x), frozen
items.text: The reflection swaps the asymptotes: horizontal floor becomes vertical wall, domain and range trade axes.

items.caption: ln(x) and eˣ, frozen
items.text: The same pair viewed from the other end — now the blue curve owns the wall and the amber one the floor.

items.secTitle: The Quadratic and the Square Root
items.caption: x² restricted, and √x, frozen
items.text: The faded left arm is the price of invertibility: only the bold right branch reflects into the square root.

items.secTitle: The Square Root and Its Inverse
items.caption: √x and its inverse, frozen
items.text: Inverting the root lands on the parabola’s right half only — the restriction is inherited from the root’s range.

items.secTitle: The Absolute Value and Its Inverse
items.caption: |x| restricted, frozen
items.text: The kept branch of the V is just y = x, so branch, inverse, and mirror coincide; the faded arm is the discarded half.

items.caption: sin(x) on [−π/2, π/2], and arcsin, frozen
items.text: One bold rising arch of the faded wave reflects into arcsine: domain [−1, 1], principal values on the y-axis.

items.caption: cos(x) on [0, π], and arccos, frozen
items.text: Cosine’s cut is one falling sweep, so arccosine falls too — from π down to 0 across its [−1, 1] domain.

items.caption: Absolute value, frozen
items.text: Two linear pieces meeting at the origin, the filled dot swallowing the open circle: left limit, right limit, and value agree.

items.caption: Heaviside step, frozen
items.text: One boundary, two constants: the open circle at (0, −1) against the filled dot at (0, 1) is the minimal jump.

items.caption: Sign function, frozen
items.text: Three pieces including a single-point interval: the lone filled dot at the origin between two open circles.

items.caption: Sawtooth, frozen
items.text: Three parallel ramps, each restarting two units lower — two identical jump events in one window.

items.caption: Removable hole, frozen
items.text: An unbroken line except for one open circle at x = 1: both limits agree, only the value is missing.

items.caption: Jump discontinuity, frozen
items.text: Two parallel lines offset by 2: the gap between the one-sided limits is the jump height itself.
